title: Drop Nested Folders
statement:
You get a list of distinct folder paths such as "/web/src". Each path starts with / and is made of lowercase names separated by /.

Remove every folder that lies inside another folder from the list, and return the ones that remain. A folder is inside "/a/b" only if its path starts with "/a/b/": "/a/bc" is not inside "/a/b".

Return the remaining paths in any order.

examples.why: Both /web/src and /web/src/ui live inside /web. The child is listed before its parent, so order in the input does not help.
"/app/libs" starts with the text "/app/lib", but it is a sibling, not a child.

constraints: Paths contain only lowercase letters and '/', start with '/', and never end with '/'
hints: If you sort the paths as plain strings, where do the folders inside "/a" end up?
After sorting, every folder inside a kept folder comes right after it. Compare each path with the last one you kept.
Keep a path unless it starts with lastKept + "/". The trailing slash is what stops "/a/bc" from matching "/a/b".

explain.intuition:
Sort the paths as strings. A parent is a prefix of its children, so it sorts before them. And because '/' sorts before every letter, all the descendants of a folder come in one block right after it, before any sibling like "/ab". So you only ever need to compare a path with the last folder you decided to keep.

A trie over the path segments gives the same answer without sorting: insert every path split on /, mark where paths end, then walk down and stop at the first marked node on each branch. It is the same idea as a router matching URL segments rather than raw characters.
steps: Walk them in order, holding last, the most recent kept path.
If the current path starts with last + "/", skip it: it lives inside last.
Otherwise keep it and make it the new last.
pitfalls: Checking startsWith(last) without the trailing slash. Then "/app/libs" is wrongly dropped as a child of "/app/lib".
Comparing with the previous path instead of the last kept one. In sorted order "/a", "/a/b", "/a/c", the last path is not inside "/a/b", but it is inside "/a" and must go.
Assuming parents come before children in the input. They do not, so sort first.

complexity.time: O(n · L · log n) for the sort, L = path length

solutions.title: Check every pair
solutions.idea: Drop a path if any other path plus a slash is a prefix of it.

solutions.title: Sort, then compare with the last kept folder
solutions.idea: Sorting puts every descendant directly after its ancestor, so one prefix check per path is enough.

solutions.title: Trie of path segments
solutions.idea: Insert each path segment by segment and mark the end. Then collect the first marked node on every branch; anything below it is nested.

followups: Folders are now added and removed one at a time, and you must answer "is this path covered by a listed folder?" quickly. Which structure do you keep?
Paths may contain "." and ".." segments. What must you do before comparing them?
